title: Death of a Pig
author: E.B. White
citation: White, E.B. 'Death of a Pig.' The Atlantic Monthly, Jan. 1948, pp. 28–33.

sections.heading: Death of a Pig: Sections 1–4

epigraph.quote: Once in a while something slips—one of the actors misreads his part, or the curtain drops too early.

paragraphs: I spent several days and nights in mid-September with an ailing pig and I feel driven to account for this stretch of time, more particularly since the pig died at last, and I lived, and things might easily have gone the other way round and none left to write the tale. By rights the pig should have been bought, say, in April, fed through the summer, and had its throat cut with traditional ceremonies in the freezing days of early winter—a classic performance following a timeless script.

The classic script is a familiar one to every countryman. The pig is purchased as a weanling, lives in comfort in his pen, eats pig meal and table scraps, grows round and sleek, and in November or December meets his end with a single thrust of a sharp knife, yielding lard, bacon, pork chops, and sausage. The farmer plays the role of murderer, but the murder is sanitized by centuries of domestic routine. The murderer loves his victim, strokes his back with a cob, feeds him milk from a pail, and then dispatches him without malice.

Once in a while something slips—one of the actors misreads his part, or the curtain drops too early. My pig fell sick in September, a premature deviation from the classic tragedy. He refused his food, his ears drooped, and an ominous listlessness settled over his pen. The classic tragedy had collapsed into a pathetic emergency.

I rushed to the telephone and summoned the veterinary. But in the country, a veterinary lives miles away and has cows and horses to attend before he can bother with a pig. I bought two ounces of castor oil, borrowed a syringe, and began an agonizing vigil in the pigpen, administering medicines, taking the pig's temperature with a human clinical thermometer, and watching his labored breathing under the pale autumn stars.

The drama became an absurd mixture of high farce and deep grief. I found myself carrying blankets to the sty, whispering words of encouragement into the animal's ear, and bargaining with fate. For four days the boundary between species dissolved. I was no longer an objective farmer tending livestock; I was a companion in suffering, bound to this small, doomed creature by the universal dread of death.

When the pig finally died, on a gray afternoon with rain falling gently through the apple trees, I experienced an acute sense of bereavement. We buried him under a pine tree at the edge of the pasture. The classic tragedy had failed, but in its failure it had exposed the fragile, mysterious, and sorrowful contract that connects human life to the animal world.
